speakers: Kyle Bass (founder Hayman Capital, hedge fund investor)
summary: Kyle Bass on how he found the subprime, Japan and sovereign debt trades by following leverage to balance sheets, and his geopolitical view that China will move on Taiwan within years. Concludes the US is the best long-term equity market and China and Europe are poor places for capital.

coverage.note: intro, host bio, Bass background: nothing actionable

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: everyone knew the housing market was overcooked. Everyone knew that it was really easy to borrow money.
claims.claim: Obvious signs of loose credit (loans to people without jobs, a bartender with three mortgages) signalled a housing bubble whose size depended on how much risk capital sat in disassociated, levered structures.
claims.indicator: anecdotal credit-availability signals; size of levered risk capital
claims.conditions: late-cycle credit boom with lending standards abandoned

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: I'm thinking, you know, it's crazy that a bartender can have three loans.
claims.claim: A non-professional borrower holding several mortgages is a street-level confirmation of speculative excess in housing credit.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: levered hedge funds just blow up well that's fine uh that's not a really systemic problem
claims.claim: Leverage losses at hedge funds are not systemic; the question that matters is what the same assets do to heavily levered banks (Lehman 36x, Bear 29x).
claims.direction: short levered banks holding the risky assets
claims.conditions: systemic only when the levered holders are banks
claims.testable: partly - leverage ratios are observable but timing is not

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: I think again uh on Wall Street you only need to get like 55% of those right, John.
claims.claim: In handicapping special situations you only need roughly 55% of outcomes right to win on Wall Street, so deep analysis of players and incentives pays.
claims.testable: partly - hit rate can be measured but 55% is an assertion

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: you lever yourself 30x and you get and you find and you end up owning assets that lose, you know, 40% of their value
claims.claim: A 30x levered balance sheet holding assets that fall 40% is wiped out arithmetically; the housing bust was a math problem for banks.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: I would say, explain to me how I'm wrong, please.
claims.claim: Before committing to a contrarian macro thesis he sought out the Fed and academics such as Rogoff and asked them to refute it.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: you had to follow the bad private assets to public balance sheets.
claims.claim: In a banking crisis the analysis shifts from private to sovereign balance sheets: ask which public balance sheet can absorb the transferred bad assets.
claims.direction: short weak sovereigns after bank bailouts
claims.conditions: depends on size of banking system relative to GDP and ability to recapitalise

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: We lost about 800 billion. So our banking system had a trillion of equity back in 2006.
claims.claim: The US could absorb about $800bn of bank losses (banking assets about 1x GDP, equity about $1tn) by recapitalising with common and preferred equity, while Europe could not.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: Iceland and Ireland both had 10 times their system 10 times their GDP in their banking system.
claims.claim: Countries whose banking systems were about 10x GDP (Iceland, Ireland) failed in succession, followed by Greece, as the crisis moved from corporate to sovereign balance sheets.
claims.direction: short sovereign debt of countries with oversized banking systems
claims.conditions: oversized banks relative to the sovereign

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: They can never let rates move. They can't. So what does that mean? That means the currency is the is the escape valve.
claims.claim: With sovereign debt near 265% of GDP Japan cannot allow rates to rise, so the yen is the adjustment valve and tends to weaken.
claims.conditions: very high sovereign debt with yield-curve control
claims.testable: partly - debt level observable, timing not

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: Either aomics has to come about and and Japan's got to inflate their way out of this problem
claims.claim: He framed Japan as a fork: reflation (Abenomics) or being crushed under debt, which justified a binary position.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: we took twothirds of the money in the fund and we bought bond market optionality right in the in JGBs.
claims.claim: He structured the Japan view as two-thirds in JGB options (bet on the bond market breaking) and one-third in a weaker-yen bet.
claims.direction: long optionality on JGBs; short yen
claims.testable: partly - structure replicable, payoff is a single case

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: we lost twothirds of the money and on the other third of the money we made many multiples of that capital.
claims.claim: Abenomics took the yen from 85 to 120; the option bet lost its premium but the yen leg returned many multiples, giving the fund about 250% overall: convex payoff when the fork resolved one way.
claims.direction: short yen won; JGB options lost

claims.speaker: John Hartley
claims.quote: feel like Japan is kind of strangely ahead of the US and the Western world maybe by you know a few decades or so.
claims.claim: Japan (asset bubble, flat GDP per capita, QE, high debt/GDP, stock buying) may be a preview of Western economies.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: I don't I think Japan's got it under control.
claims.claim: He did not see Japan as the first domino of a sovereign debt crisis.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: almost no sovereign ever defaults John they get into a crisis they print they print and print money expand a balance sheet but they always pay
claims.claim: Advanced sovereigns with own currency rarely default; they print, so the consequence is currency debasement and inflation rather than default.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: when real estate prices rip and wages don't go with them, you create yourself an endemic problem in your economy.
claims.claim: Printing and deficits inflate asset prices faster than wages, which prices young people out of housing, delaying marriage and fertility and bending demographic curves down.
claims.indicator: house prices vs wages, fertility rates

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: when home prices in China got to be 26 times median income, um the men couldn't afford homes.
claims.claim: Chinese home prices reached 26x median income, and Xi has not stimulated the property market because financial security is national security.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: real wages have been massively negative even though the Fed is not saying that. The reason the Fed's not saying that is because they chain weighted inflation.
claims.claim: Official chain-weighted inflation understates the rise in asset and housing prices, so real wages are worse than reported.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: we just injected 50% inflation in dollar terms into the world.
claims.claim: Dollar money creation raised dollar-priced prices about 50% worldwide in four years, which he links to collapsing demographics.

claims.speaker: John Hartley
claims.quote: if you look at like the K Schiller index and you you net out inflation, that trend is like basically flat from like the late 19th century, late 1800s up until like the 1970s and 80s
claims.claim: Real US house prices were flat from the late 1800s to the 1970s-80s and rose steeply afterward, so the affordability problem is recent.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: The US government's own unchain weighted housing index was up 50% between 2020 and 2024.
claims.claim: The FHFA unchained house price index rose 50% from 2020 to 2024, far above wage growth.
claims.indicator: FHFA house price index vs wages

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: And then it prices the middle class out of being mobile.
claims.claim: Asset inflation hurts the poor through food, rent and gas and immobilises the middle class, widening the gap and raising social tension.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: we should expect more and more war uh because there is no answer for for for this equation at the moment.
claims.claim: He expects more wars as inflation, asset-price gaps and falling fertility tear at social fabric while central banks keep growing balance sheets.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: I put my whole team on China and I this starts empirically with me calling all the Wall Street firms and saying someone send me your primer on the Chinese banking system.
claims.claim: He built an edge on China by studying how its closed-capital-account banking system and RMB/CNH link work.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: no Wall Street firm had a bank primer for Chinese banking system. No one had done it.
claims.claim: Sell-side research was selling Chinese stocks and VIE structures while nobody mapped the banking architecture, an information gap he exploited.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: when you understand what their grand strategy is, it is completely incompatible with ours.
claims.claim: Understanding China's system, history and incentives shows its grand strategy is incompatible with the US, so conflict is likely.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: They continue their air their air defense zone incursions into the Taiwanese air defense. And if you chart it, you can see that every year it's more belligerent.
claims.claim: Annual growth in Chinese air-defense-zone incursions into Taiwan is a chartable signal that an invasion is approaching.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: it should be obvious to you that you shouldn't rely on China for your supply chain.
claims.claim: Rare-earth magnet shortages hit firms such as Ford because they ignored a long visible risk of dependence on China.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: I think you're going to see China invade Taiwan and forever change the makeup of the economic relationship between the West and China.
claims.claim: He expects a Chinese move on Taiwan that permanently reshapes West-China economic ties.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: So this attack was obvious that it was coming.
claims.claim: Israel's strike on Iran's nuclear sites was predictable because Iran would not accept inspection of new centrifuges.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: It took their current account plus 250 billion because they shut off international travel for their population and they dialed back the school expenses.
claims.claim: China's current account was heading toward zero in late 2019 amid the Hong Kong crisis; COVID travel and tuition restrictions swung it by about $250bn, easing the external constraint.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: So the three options are soft with the KMT winning in 28.
claims.claim: He sees three routes to Taiwan: soft (KMT election win in 2028), blockade, or all-out assault; a blockade would force US action.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: They have to import their energy and their food every day.
claims.claim: Taiwan has about two weeks of energy on island, so a blockade of its ports would be effective and requires US unblocking, leading to kinetic conflict.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: lends it only to be somewhat amendable to an amphibious invasion three months out of the year
claims.claim: Taiwan's tides and terrain make an amphibious assault feasible only about three months a year, so he thinks China prefers a soft or blockade route.

claims.speaker: John Hartley
claims.quote: I think if you're investing today, if you had invested in China from that time to today, uh we'd be maybe flat or something like that.
claims.claim: Investors in China since the BRIC era 2000s-2010s would have roughly flat returns today.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: don't have a great plan for the soft power takeover.
claims.claim: The US military has plans for blockade and assault scenarios but not for a soft power takeover of Taiwan.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: Taiwan is like a Chinese democracy that's embraced Western capitalism. Taiwan's GDP per capita is 300% what China's is.
claims.claim: Taiwan shows what open capital and Western institutions could do for China, which is why it threatens Xi.
claims.indicator: GDP per capita Taiwan vs China

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: they steal 300 billionish of IP from us every year and earn earn a return on it.
claims.claim: Chinese economic statecraft (IP theft estimated at $300bn a year, VC infiltration) makes China an adversary rather than a trading partner.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: We're not talking about, hey, you know, you charge us this tariff on agriculture and we charge this on cars.
claims.claim: Rare-earth coercion makes US-China talks a hostage negotiation rather than a trade negotiation, so a positive economic relationship cannot be expected.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: Xi Jinping move in the next two or three years on Taiwan.
claims.claim: He expects a Chinese move on Taiwan within two to three years with direct US involvement and possible strikes on Fujian installations.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: if you believe that China is our enemy and that we might be at a kinetic conflict with China in the coming years, why on earth would you invest dollars in anything Chinese?
claims.claim: Conflict risk means US investors should not own Chinese assets; investing in communism has not worked long term.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: At some point in time, it became a bad bet and we must admit it
claims.claim: China exposure was a good bet when westernisation was expected to lift productivity, but turned bad when that assumption failed.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: Their banking system is 320% of their GDP. There are two Chinese banks that have more assets than JP Morgan.
claims.claim: China's banking system (320% of GDP, giant banks, closed capital account) is architecturally flawed, so regime instability is likely.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: We we have their ticket into the world financial system.
claims.claim: If China moves on Taiwan the US can hobble it financially via dollar access and sanctions on its four SOE and twelve joint stock banks.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: that's that's likely the progression of that regime's exit when if and when he goes kinetic.
claims.claim: Financial hobbling after a Taiwan attack would make it hard for Xi to hang on, so regime change is likely.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: China with a limitless partnership with the war criminal in Russia.
claims.claim: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea are cooperating as an authoritarian axis this time.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: the Biden administration made a huge blunder with the uh turning our back on Saudi Arabia and embracing Iran.
claims.claim: US policy turning from Saudi toward Iran was a blunder; Saudi and the UAE are principal US allies.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: as of Q1 of 2024 uh you saw the UAE decide to align themselves with the US and and walk away from China
claims.claim: The UAE (G42) realigned with the US away from China, a positive development for US-Gulf ties and the Abraham Accords.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: my view on October 7th is that was to disrupt uh the Abraham Accords from moving forward
claims.claim: He thinks the October 7 attack aimed to derail the Abraham Accords, which he expects will still proceed.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: The world's priced in dollars, John. We just pushed 50% dollar inflation to the world in a four-year period. And they have a negative convexity to us.
claims.claim: Dollar-priced inflation hits import-dependent countries hardest and their stress escalates into kinetic conflict before it deescalates.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: Because people vote with their money. We have the most liquid, best, deepest capital markets in the world.
claims.claim: The US (4% of population, 26% of GDP, 60% of world capital markets) is the best place for long-term capital because of its deep liquid markets and entrepreneurship.
claims.indicator: US share of world GDP and market cap
claims.testable: partly - shares measurable, conclusion is judgment

claims.speaker: John Hartley
claims.quote: I think if if you were to strip out all these tech companies from the US, the US would probably look pretty much like the rest of the West.
claims.claim: US outperformance and flat GDP per capita elsewhere is driven largely by tech, and EU regulation holds European tech back.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: that gap between the wealthy, the middle class, and the and the poor continues to grow because we're going to keep running $1.8 trillion deficits going forward.
claims.claim: The caveat to US investing is persistent $1.8tn deficits that widen the wealth gap and increase friction.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: uh to your point on Europe with GDPR and some of the foot their own own goals that Europe scores on themselves
claims.claim: Europe's regulation (GDPR) and repeated self-inflicted policy errors make it a poor place to deploy capital.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: you've lost a third of your money and they've grown their economy 505%.
claims.claim: An investor in the CSI 300 18 years ago lost a third of capital while China's GDP grew 505%, so GDP growth in a state-controlled economy does not accrue to foreign shareholders.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: But I'm not interested in picking up dimes in front of bulldozers.
claims.claim: He avoids short-term trading in structurally risky markets and prefers long-term investments in companies that can succeed.

claims.speaker: Kyle Bass
claims.quote: they have no fiscal union. They have no central taxing authority.
claims.claim: Europe lacks fiscal union, central taxing authority, a joint military and deposit guarantee; under stress it will break, so it is an idea not a union.

claims.speaker: John Hartley
claims.quote: the USSR was going to you know eclipse the US and growth and then uh it was uh Japan uh in the 1980s and then you know China in the 2000s
claims.claim: Repeated forecasts that the USSR, Japan or China would overtake the US failed, so betting against the US has been a bad strategy.
